extracted.intended_audience: the people of the State of New York; citizens/voters deliberating the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical arguments for structuring the federal government’s powers, institutions, and procedures (defense, judiciary, legislature, ratification) to preserve the Union and ensure effective national administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive concurrence requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The text argues against requiring very large majorities for national acts, warning that when "the concurrence of a large number is required" it "gives greater scope to foreign corruption, as well as to domestic faction" and allows obstruction of necessary government action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and rationale: in wartime an ally or enemy could bribe a smaller set required by a supermajority to prevent peace; high supermajority rules make it easier for foreign powers or private interests to 'tie up the hands of government.' The implicit criterion: prefer decision rules that do not unduly empower obstruction (e.g., avoid two-thirds requirements where a simple majority suffices for essential national acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a national supreme judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: "A circumstance which crowns the defects of the Confederation remains yet to be mentioned, the want of a judiciary power." Treaties and laws need courts to "expound and define their true meaning and operation," and to produce uniformity there ought to be one "SUPREME TRIBUNAL."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: the supreme tribunal must be instituted under the same authority that forms treaties; without it there will be contradictory final determinations from state courts, bias from local views, and continual infractions of federal obligations. Purpose: ensure uniform rule of civil justice and protect national interests from local prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal laws should bind individuals directly (not rely solely on states)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay contends the Union must "extend the laws of the federal government to the individual citizens of America; we must discard the fallacious scheme of quotas and requisitions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: relying on state legislatures or requisitions has proven impracticable and unjust; direct federal authority prevents failure of execution and avoids dependence on states' goodwill or ability to comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification must rest on the consent of the people, not only legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution ought to rest on "the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE." The existing Confederation's ratification by state legislatures exposes federal powers to questions (including the doctrine of repeal by a party to a compact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: foundations of national government should be deeper than delegated authority from state legislatures; popular ratification secures legitimacy and prevents unilateral repeal by a party to the compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant federal government powers commensurate to its entrusted objects (means proportioned to ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle stated plainly: "the MEANS ought to be proportioned to the END; the persons, from whose agency the attainment of any END is expected, ought to possess the MEANS by which it is to be attained."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: once it is decided a federal government is needed for common defense/commerce/etc., it must be 'clothed with all the powers requisite to complete execution of its trust.' Do not impose constitutional shackles that prevent effective fulfillment of national duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal control of military establishments and defense powers must be broad and flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities essential to common defense ("to raise armies; to build and equip fleets; to prescribe rules for the government of both; to direct their operations; to provide for their support") "ought to exist without limitation, BECAUSE IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO FORESEE OR DEFINE THE EXTENT AND VARIETY OF NATIONAL EXIGENCIES."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: national exigencies are infinite; constitutionally rigid limits on defense powers would cripple response to unforeseen threats. The criterion supports broad discretionary authority for formation, direction, and support of national forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government must be empowered to levy troops and raise revenues directly
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union "ought to be invested with full power to levy troops; to build and equip fleets; and to raise the revenues which will be required for the formation and support of an army and navy, in the customary and ordinary modes practiced in other governments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejects quotas/requisition schemes and requires ordinary governmental fiscal and military mechanisms (direct levies, revenue-raising) to ensure execution of national defense and other federal functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid entrusting military forces to individual states
rubrics_metrics.description: Separately held state military forces would produce rivalry, jealousy, and make military establishments "engines for the abridgment or demolition of the national authority." The framers of the Confederation prohibited states having ships or troops without Congress's consent for this reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design implication: national security requires that the federal government, rather than individual states, hold effective military power; dispersing forces risks uneven burdens, escalation, and threats to the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt impracticable absolute constitutional prohibitions on standing armies in peacetime
rubrics_metrics.description: The objection to standing armies in peacetime is characterized as "vague and general," and the author argues that restraints on legislative discretion regarding military establishments "would be improper to be imposed, and if imposed, from the necessities of society, would be unlikely to be observed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of absolute bans, practical checks (e.g., fiscal controls) are preferred. Example: the proposed plan forbids appropriation for army support for longer than two years — a 'great and real security' against unnecessarily permanent standing armies while preserving necessary legislative discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: National provision for frontier posts, garrisons, and naval infrastructure is necessary for security and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a commercial people and secure on the Atlantic side the nation must have a navy; this requires dock-yards and arsenals and, for their defense, "fortifications, and probably garrisons."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: frontier garrisons are indispensable against Indian depredations; dockyards and arsenals need protection until naval power matures. Practical implication: federal powers should permit establishment and defense of such infrastructure where necessary for trade and national security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute objects of government to appropriate departments with commensurate authority
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the circumstances of our country are such as to demand a compound instead of a simple... government, the essential point... will be to discriminate the OBJECTS... which shall appertain to the different provinces or departments of power; allowing to each the most ample authority for fulfilling the objects committed to its charge."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rule: clearly allocate subjects (defense, commerce, administration of justice) to the appropriate level (federal vs state) and ensure each has powers sufficient to accomplish its designated ends; failing to do so is a violation of prudence and will lead to malfunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversaries must show defects in internal structure, not merely declaim about extent of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The author argues critics should have confined themselves to demonstrating that "the internal structure of the proposed government was such as to render it unworthy of the confidence of the people" rather than making "inflammatory declamations... about the extent of the powers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard: critiques of a constitutional plan should address concrete defects in organization or safeguards, not only assert that powers are 'too extensive' in the abstract; substantive structural criticisms are required to justify rejection.
